https://www.dw.com/en/alaska-charter-fli.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JBH8 Six passengers and two pilots were aboard the plane during the incident [Representative image] Image: Hohlfeld/IMAGO Advertisement A charter plane crash at a remote military radar site in western Alaska on Thursday has left all eight people on board dead, according to the United States military. The aircraft crashed around 12:15 pm (2015 UTC) on approach to Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site Airport, located about 725 kilometers (450 miles) west of Anchorage, Alaska's largest city, from where it had departed. Six passengers and two pilots were aboard the plane during the incident, said Clint Johnson, Alaska region chief of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB). Reports identified the plane as a ‌Cessna 441 operated by Anchorage-based air charter company Security Aviation. Alaska Senator Lisa Murkowski expressed her condolences, following news of the crash. "I've traveled extensively with Security Aviation throughout Alaska, and have met many of their experienced pilots," she said on X, naming the charter company that operates in the remote region. She added that multiple agencies, including the US Coast Guard, NTSB, Alaska State Troopers, and the Rescue Coordination Center had responded to the crash. Air Force Alaskan Command mourns 'loss for our military family' The Associated Press cited the US ​military's Alaskan Command as saying that the plane was a "civilian-contracted aircraft." The passengers on board were "dedicated professionals carrying out a vital mission in a demanding environment," AP quoted Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, commander of Alaskan Command, the Alaskan North American Aerospace Defense Command Region and Eleventh Air Force, as saying in a statement. The specifics of what work the crash victims were doing at the radar site — which tracks aircraft operating in Alaskan airspace — was not immediately clear from the Alaskan Command's statement. "This is a devastating loss for our military family and the communities we serve," Davis said, according to AP. The Pacific Air Forces Regional Support Center manages the radar site. https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/09/23/eu-e.text: Menü Kereső Az EP jelentéstevője is megszólalt a magyar feltételességi eljárásról, de ő másért felel Külföld Márton Balázs Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom El kell ismerni a haladást Magyarországon, de az eurómilliárdokat csak megvalósított reformokra szabad odaadni, figyelmeztetett szerdán Tineke Strik. Az Európai Parlament (EP) képviselője azután adott ki egy közleményt, hogy az Európai Bizottság javasolta : szüntessék meg a 4,2 milliárd eurót (mostani árfolyamon több mint 1500 milliárd forintot) befagyasztó feltételességi jogállamisági eljárást. Strik elvárta, hogy az Európai Bizottság magyarázza meg, miért látta úgy, hogy az uniós költségvetésre leselkedő veszélyeket megfelelően kezelték, miközben még mindig tartanak olyan fontos reformok, mint például a közérdekű vagyonkezelő alapítványok (kekvák) kivezetése. Ahogy arról korábban is írtunk , a feltételességi eljárásban eleve nem várták el a kekvák megszüntetését, csak az átláthatósági és összeférhetetlenségi problémáik kezelését. A Tisza-kormány első körben azokat a kekvákat szüntette meg, amelyek nem modellváltó egyetemek mögött állnak. A többiekre ideiglenesen bevezette azokat a reformokat, amelyeket az Európai Bizottság 2024 végén sorolt fel , és amelyeket utána meg sem próbált végrehajtani az előző kormány. Kicsoda, bocsánat? Strik véleményét több lap is átvette az MTI-n keresztül, például a Mediaworkshöz tartozó Világgazdaság „Erre nem számított Magyar Péter: fontos brüsszeli politikus támadt rá Ursula von der Leyenre, mert uniós pénzt adott Magyarországnak” címmel. A holland zöldpárti képviselő valamit valóban befolyásolhat közvetlenül, csak éppen nem a feltételességi eljárást, ahogy maga az EP sem. Áprilisban, Magyar Péter választás utáni állami médiás interjújában ugyanezt játszották el, amikor „Brüsszel kétséges válaszaként” hivatkoztak Strik és egy másik EP-képviselő akkori szavaira. „Kicsoda, bocsánat?” – kérdezett vissza Magyar, arra utalva, hogy az EP nem vesz részt közvetlenül sem ebben, sem más eljárásban, amely uniós pénzt fagyaszt be. (Az interjúztató, Csete Beáta azóta az ellenzéki pártok szakértőinek fenntartott páholyban tűnt fel .) Az eljárást a tagállami kormányokat képviselő Tanács szüntetheti meg, ahogy az elindításáról is ez a testület döntött 27-ből 25 igennel. Erre a bizottsági javaslat után alapesetben egy hónapja lesz. Strik közleménye erre utalva megjegyezte, hogy a Tanácsnak kell elemeznie a bizottsági javaslatot, és „elvárom, hogy a Parlamentet is teljes mértékben, részletesen informálják a feltételességi rendeletnek megfelelően”. (A jogszabály szerint az Európai Bizottságnak „minden intézkedésről tájékoztatnia kell az Európai Parlamentet”, de ennél szigorúbb kötelezettséget nem ír elő az EP felé.) Striknek valóban van egy befolyásosabb pozíciója: ő felel az EP-ben jelentéstevőként a „hetes cikkes” magyar eljárásért . Ez az uniós értékekről szól, nem csak arról, hol veszélyeztetheti a jogállamisági helyzet az uniós forrásokat. Strik szerdai közleménye is utalt rá, hogy ez „szélesebb körű reformokat” igényel. Ezt az eljárást az EP kezdeményezte, és egy korábbi példa alapján úgy tűnik, a képviselő-testület is szüntetethetné meg, valamint a továbblépésnél is lenne szerepe. A végén bizonyos uniós jogokat lehetne vele felfüggeszteni, de ennek még a közelében sincsenek, az eljárás 2018-as megindítása óta nem halad se előre, se hátra. Strikkel májusban interjúztunk . Akkor azt mondta, a tervek szerint októberben egy EP-küldöttség érkezik Magyarországra. Az lesz „a tökéletes pillanat, hogy az érintettekkel egyeztessünk”: elégedettek-e azzal, ahogyan a dolgok a gyakorlatban működnek. „Talán ez vezethet a jelentésünkhöz egy visszavonási javaslattal.” Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Many residents are concerned about the health and environmental issues a datacenter could bring to the community. Photograph: Gina Ferazzi View image in fullscreen Imperial, California, at dusk in March. Many residents are concerned about the health and environmental issues a datacenter could bring to the community. Photograph: Gina Ferazzi California Inside the long, bitter fight over one man’s quest to build the biggest AI datacenter in California A modern-day prospector promised rural Imperial thousands of jobs and millions in tax revenue – but his plan has set off a firestorm of resistance Dara Kerr and Gabrielle Canon Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.01 EDT Share Sebastian Rucci zoomed in on a map in late 2024, looking closely at a large block of brown earth. The barren plot sandwiched between sprawling alfalfa fields and sleepy desert suburbs was exactly what he’d been searching for – the perfect place to realize his dream of building the largest artificial intelligence datacenter in California . The dusty expanse wasn’t an obvious location. It was in the Sonoran desert, just north of the Mexican border, where temperatures regularly rose past 100F (37.8C). Water was scarce in the once-booming agricultural area, which gets its supply from the beleaguered Colorado River. And then, there was the city of Imperial – population 22,000 – to win over. As controversial datacenter projects have sprung up across the US, residents were naturally skeptical of a new, energy-guzzling neighbor. But for Rucci, a 66-year-old lawyer with a complicated past, none of these obstacles seemed insurmountable. Rucci is among the new class of middlemen who inhabit the burgeoning world of datacenter development. The rapid rise of artificial intelligence – galvanized by Silicon Valley companies worth trillions of dollars – has fueled one of the biggest industrial construction booms in history. The technology requires far more computing power than traditional internet services, and that means building enormous new structures to house millions of servers. View image in fullscreen A portrait of Sebastian Rucci at the location of his proposed AI data center, Imperial, California, on 1 July 2026. Photograph: John Francis Peters This proliferation of datacenters is now attracting modern-day prospectors seeking land in hopes of cashing in on one of the fastest-growing and most lucrative industries on Earth. Set in their sights are areas like Imperial county : rural, underdeveloped and desperate for an economic boost. “I didn’t know much about datacenters,” Rucci said, recalling a couple of years back. “I made calls to people I knew in Silicon Valley. And within a short period, I realized: holy shit, this stuff is huge.” Rucci, a self-described expert at doing the tedious legwork of packaging permits and plans, proved adept at selling a bright future of economic development to county lawmakers. He said his sales skills also nabbed him a direct line to Google, which floated interest in being the tenant of the datacenter, according to emails between Rucci and county agencies. With the promise of these potential partnerships and support from construction unions , Rucci moved into high gear last year and began plotting his nearly 1m-square-foot datacenter – a facility the size of 16 football fields combined. He said he had invested about $5m already, and, if it gets approved and passed off to a builder, he expects “big multipliers of that” in return. What Rucci didn’t expect, however, was the firestorm of resistance his project set off in the community . Over the past year, more than half a dozen lawsuits have been filed, along with recall efforts for local officials who supported the project. Even a temporary 45-day datacenter moratorium was approved. Echoing similar battles against such development across the US, Imperial county residents told the Guardian they fear increased emissions, harm to the region’s rare desert wildlife, constraints on the power grid and rapidly dwindling water supply, along with noise issues. Rucci denies the project will have such effects. View image in fullscreen Demonstrators wave signs during a nationwide protest against AI datacenter expansion in Imperial. Photograph: Sandy Huffaker/AFP/Getty Images It seems the backlash succeeded – for now. Rucci’s developments are on pause after a county judge ruled last month that his project cannot move forward until it clears an extensive environmental review. Despite a bold start, Rucci could end up a cautionary tale of what can go wrong when a businessman moves too fast without community buy-in. “This project was presented as a Noah’s Ark that’s going to come save everybody,” said Francisco Leal, who lives in a residential neighborhood across the street from Rucci’s proposed datacenter. “But the community sees this project as a Trojan horse.” From strip club owner to datacenter developer When Rucci landed on that vast plot of land in Imperial county in late 2024, only two things really mattered: finding a location that could be exempted from California’s strict environmental building requirements, and getting his hands on a lot of electricity. In unincorporated Imperial county, he had both. Because the land was zoned for industrial use, he was able to apply for an exemption from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), which would fast-track the project by avoiding the environmental permitting process. And for electricity, Rucci was able to work with the local energy provider to eventually get 330 megawatts of electricity – enough to power a city the size of Tallahassee. Satellite map of a proposed datacenter in Imperial, California Rucci is based in Huntington Beach, but has started several businesses throughout southern California, St Louis and Ohio. In early 2025, he said one of his connections introduced him to a longtime Google employee who helped guide him through the process. In a July email to Imperial county’s planning and development services, Rucci wrote that the datacenter would “enable Google to conduct artificial intelligence and large language model training for its Gemini system”, Google’s suite of AI models. “We have secured interest from Google for this project, which we are confident will transform the area through increased tax revenues, new employment opportunities, and expanded energy production,” Rucci wrote in another email in August to the county’s air pollution control district. “We are not involved in a datacenter project in Imperial county,” said a Google spokesperson. She did not respond to questions about the company’s relationship with Rucci. He said Google’s response made sense considering they do not have a formal agreement. While California has dozens of datacenters capable of cloud computing, streaming and internet searches, the state has scant facilities dedicated to AI. That’s because California is one of the most rigorous states when it comes to environmental permitting for energy and water-intensive facilities such as AI datacenters. View image in fullscreen No Data Center signs are posted in the front yard of a home which is right behind the proposed site for a 950,000 sq ft data center on 12 March in Imperial. Photograph: Gina Ferazzi/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images Major projects in California take an average of seven years to get completed, said Michael Thomas, the founder of Cleanview , which tracks datacenter development. For comparison, the average in Texas is about three years. Thomas said he had seen a surge of new players, like Rucci, get into AI datacenter development nationwide. These people, he said, were willing to take on the risk and find ways to speed up the process. “Land and power have become so scarce at the scale that these big tech companies need,” Thomas said. So, if a developer can shorten the timeline, “a company like Google or Microsoft or Meta may be willing to pay you a huge premium … It’s potentially a way to make millions of dollars very quickly.” Rucci is no stranger to taking on risk. He has owned a strip club, addiction treatment centers and dozens of accounting and real estate endeavors. In 2010, while operating the strip club, Go Go Cabaret, he was convicted on four counts of illegal liquor sales for which he had to serve a 30-day jail sentence. He was also charged with engaging in a pattern of corrupt activity, money laundering and promoting prostitution, but those charges were later dismissed. In 2019, California suspended his license to practice law for nearly three years. He has also filed for corporate bankruptcy at least twice. The most recent time, in 2023, took place after the Department of Justice investigated one of his addiction treatment centers for alleged fraud, ending with a government seizure of $600,000 of assets. No criminal charges were filed, however, and that money was later returned with interest after Rucci sued the government to reclaim the seized funds. Since zeroing in on Imperial county in 2024, Rucci has registered several new businesses related to the vast datacenter campus, from construction and energy supply to ongoing operations. The umbrella company for his project is an LLC called Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing (IVCM). Rucci says the facility will bring in more than 1,600 construction jobs and nearly $30m in annual tax revenue. It will also include an electrical substation, on-site battery energy storage and more than 130 methane-gas-fueled generators, according to an application submitted to the county planning department. Rucci said his diverse experience was well-suited for such a complicated project. “That doesn’t mean that my background isn’t colorful,” he said. “I’ve challenged cities. I fought the federal government. I’ve done a lot of stuff. But that doesn’t mean that I don’t know how to process this and get it through.” Battle lines At first, Leal had no clue that the dusty 75 acres of land across the street from his house had been bought by a developer. It wasn’t until the day before Thanksgiving last year when he found a colorful flyer hanging from his door that his world began to swirl around him. The flyer mapped out the huge project and warned that construction was moving forward without requiring the state’s usual environmental review. Leal began scanning the internet, and what he found shocked him. His back fence was all that separated his home from Rucci’s property. While Leal lived in Imperial city, the datacenter would fall just outside city limits on unincorporated county land. It was clear that living next to this facility would permanently change the quiet life he and his wife had envisioned when they moved there some 20 years earlier. “When we bought that house, we planned for it to be the house where we would retire, where our kids would grow up and return when they visit,” Leal said. “The quality of life of anybody living half a mile from the datacenter will be affected.” He started texting his neighbors that same day. As word spread, people began to organize, holding meetings and rallies against the datacenter proposal. Within months, close to 3,500 people would sign a petition opposing the facility, and state senator Steve Padilla, who represents the district, would sound the alarm , introducing a series of bills aimed at datacenters. View image in fullscreen Residents protest against the plans for a new datacenter. Photograph: Courtesy of Valle Imperial Resiste As AI datacenters have popped up around the world, they’ve come under scrutiny for being extremely resource-intensive. A query through chatbots such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Google’s Gemini needs nearly 10 times as much electricity as a typical internet search, and that number can increase for more complicated prompts. Because supercomputers run hot, they typically need extensive water-cooling systems. Imperial county is a critical habitat for wildlife like the desert pupfish, which is listed as an endangered species under the California Endangered Species Act and swims through agricultural drains and canals, much like one that crosses Rucci’s property. Other desert animals of concern include the flat-tailed horned lizard, yellow-breasted chat and burrowing owls. As Leal got more involved in the datacenter fight, he met other concerned residents, like Christopher Scurries. Scurries lives nearby and is a music teacher at Imperial high school. He said he was worried about datacenter noise, what’s known as a constant low hum. “I’ll definitely hear when I’m here in my house,” he said. Scurries and his wife moved to the area in 2017 so they could afford a home. Now with a two-year-old daughter, his previously pleasant life feels uncertain in the shadow of the datacenter. It’s testament to a long-simmering sentiment in this corner of the Sonoran desert, where pollutants from agriculture and industry, along with poverty, have long taken an undue toll. One in five adults is unemployed in the region and the poverty rate, at close to 20%, is the highest in California. “The benefits these structures may bring into a community – the jobs, tax revenue, even the infrastructure improvements – may feel uncertain or uneven compared to the scale of the impact,” said Carla Walker, the US director of environmental justice and equity at the research organization World Resources Institute. “Communities are asking these questions of who benefits and who pays the price.” For Jacob Rodriguez, who was born and raised in the area, who pays the price has been top of mind. “It’s an existential threat,” he said of the datacenter project, noting that residents had long dealt with pollution and dwindling water supplies. “The respiratory problems and the air quality here are already abysmal … eventually, indirectly, this will cost lives.” ‘I’m not here to run for Miss America’ By March, tensions between Rucci and the community had reached a boiling point. At an Imperial county board of supervisors meeting, dozens of residents, including Leal and Scurries, packed into the chambers for a public feedback session. As Rucci stood at the lectern, trying to present his more than 100 slides on the project, the crowd steadily chanted “no datacenters” and waved “not in my backyard” signs. It got so raucous that Rucci, the main speaker on the schedule , left the meeting early. As he walked out of the building, protesters yelled “Fuera, Rucci, fuera” (“leave” in Spanish). Visibly fed up, Rucci unexpectedly approached a person screaming through a bullhorn and roared in their face. Tensions grew heated between Rucci and community members during a meeting in March. By this point, the project was at the center of a heated legal battle. The city of Imperial had sued the county for bypassing public input and environmental reviews when it approved the datacenter (the environmental nonprofit Sierra Club later joined on). Rucci, in turn, counter-sued in federal court on behalf of his company IVCM, alleging the city carried out a “bad-faith campaign of administrative obstruction and targeted retaliation”. He then went on to sue an anti-datacenter activist named Jake Tison, the Comité Cívico del Valle non-profit, and its executive director, Luis Olmedo, and the local public-media news station KPBS and one of its reporters, Kori Suzuki, for defamation. Those three defamation suits were dismissed. Rucci has appealed in the cases against KPBS and Comité Cívico del Valle and is working to reverse the ruling on Tison. “Look, I’m not here to run for Miss America or Mr America,” Rucci said. “I’m here to do a datacenter.” Rucci, on behalf of IVCM, also sued the local utility , the Imperial irrigation district, for rejecting an application for water to cool the datacenter. https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/actualitate/.text: Parlamentul României găzduieşte în perioada 10-12 noiembrie 2026 un program de formare în domeniul inteligenţei artificiale, organizat cu sprijinul Organizaţiei Naţiunilor Unite, prin Programul Naţiunilor Unite pentru Dezvoltare (UNDP). Deputatul PNL Andrei Baciu, inițiator al programului, argumentează că parlamentarii nu pot legifera un domeniu pe care nu îl înțeleg. „Este un proiect pe care l-am iniţiat în urmă cu aproximativ şase luni şi pentru a cărui concretizare am purtat discuţii şi am făcut demersuri directe la nivelul leadershipului ONU, la New York şi Geneva. Ideea a pornit de la o nevoie concretă: Parlamentul României trebuie să fie pregătit să înţeleagă transformările generate de inteligenţa artificială şi să aibă capacitatea de a lua decizii legislative informate într-un domeniu care evoluează foarte rapid. Am propus acest program în cadrul discuţiilor de la sediul central al ONU din New York, iar în această vară am reuşit să confirm proiectul în urma întâlnirilor de la Geneva. Ulterior, am lucrat împreună cu reprezentanţii UNDP şi cu echipele Camerei Deputaţilor şi Senatului pentru a transforma această iniţiativă într-un program concret, dedicat parlamentarilor şi personalului parlamentar”, a declarat deputatul Andrei Baciu, potrivit unui comunicat de presă. Programul va fi susţinut de doi experţi internaţionali ai UNDP, care au venit special la Bucureşti din New York şi Singapore: „Consider că această pregătire este esenţială. Inteligenţa artificială nu mai este o tehnologie a viitorului, ci o realitate care influenţează deja viaţa cetăţenilor, economia, piaţa muncii, educaţia, sănătatea şi funcţionarea instituţiilor publice. În acelaşi timp, apar provocări majore legate de dezinformare, manipularea prin deepfake, protecţia datelor, securitatea cibernetică şi respectarea drepturilor fundamentale. Toate acestea au implicaţii directe asupra democraţiei, securităţii naţionale şi procesului legislativ. Ca legiuitori, avem responsabilitatea să înţelegem aceste schimbări şi să fim capabili să construim un cadru legislativ adaptat noilor realităţi. Nu putem reglementa eficient o tehnologie pe care nu o înţelegem. Mă bucur că am reuşit să aduc acest program în Parlamentul României şi că putem beneficia de expertiza unor specialişti internaţionali de prim rang. Este un prim pas dintr-un demers mai amplu prin care îmi propun să aduc inteligenţa artificială în centrul dezbaterilor parlamentare şi să susţin dezvoltarea capacităţii instituţionale în acest domeniu”, a mai spus Andrei Baciu. În cadrul programului de formare, ziua de 10 noiembrie va fi dedicată membrilor Parlamentului, iar zilele de 11 şi 12 noiembrie vor fi dedicate personalului parlamentar.
